title: Part 1, Chapter 7
paragraphs: About the second sally of our worthy knight Don Quixote of La Mancha

At this instant Don Quixote began shouting out, "Here, here, valiant knights! Here is where you need to put forth the might of your strong arms, for those of the Court are gaining the upper hand in the tournament!" Called away by this noise and outcry, they got no further with the inspection of the remaining books, and so it is thought that "The Carolea," "The Lion of Spain," and "The Deeds of the Emperor," written by Don Luis de Ávila, went to the fire unseen and unheard, for they were no doubt among those that remained, and perhaps if the curate had seen them they would not have suffered so severe a sentence.
When they reached Don Quixote he was already out of bed, still shouting and raving, and slashing and cutting all round, as wide awake as if he had never slept.

They closed with him and by force got him back to bed, and once he had calmed down a little, addressing the curate he said, "Truly, Señor Archbishop Turpin, it is a great disgrace for us who call ourselves the Twelve Peers to have so carelessly let the knights of the Court win the victory in this tournament, after we adventurers had carried off the honour on the three previous days."

"Hush, friend," said the curate; "please God, the luck may turn, and what is lost today may be won tomorrow; for now, let your worship take care of your health, since it seems to me you are over-tired, if not badly wounded."

"Wounded, no," said Don Quixote, "but bruised and battered, no doubt, for that bastard Don Roland has cudgelled me with the trunk of an oak tree, and all out of envy, because he sees that I alone rival him in his achievements. But I should not call myself Reinaldos of Montalvan if he does not pay me for it in spite of all his enchantments as soon as I rise from this bed. For now, let them bring me something to eat, for that, I feel, is what would most serve my purpose, and leave the avenging to me."
They did as he wished; they gave him something to eat, and once more he fell asleep, leaving them marvelling at his madness.

That night the housekeeper burnt to ashes all the books that were in the yard and in the whole house, and some must have gone up that deserved preservation in lasting archives; but their fate, and the laziness of the inspector, did not allow it, and so in them was verified the proverb that the innocent suffer for the guilty.

One of the remedies the curate and the barber immediately applied to their friend's disorder was to wall up and plaster over the room where the books had been, so that when he got up he wouldn't find it (the idea being that, the cause removed, the effect might cease), and they would say that some magician had carried it off, room and all. This was done with all dispatch. Two days later Don Quixote got up, and the first thing he did was go and look at his books; and not finding the room where he had left it, he wandered from side to side looking for it. He came to the place where the door had been, and felt at it with his hands, and turned and twisted his eyes in every direction without saying a word; but after a long while he asked his housekeeper whereabouts the room that held his books was.

The housekeeper, who had been well coached in what to answer, said, "What room, or what nothing, is your worship looking for? There is neither room nor books in this house now, for the devil himself has carried it all away."

"It was not the devil," said the niece, "but a magician who came on a cloud one night, the day after your worship left, and dismounting from a serpent he rode he entered the room — what he did in there I don't know — but after a little while he made off, flying through the roof, and left the house full of smoke; and when we went to see what he had done, we found neither book nor room. But the housekeeper and I remember very well that on leaving, the old villain said in a loud voice that, for a private grudge he owed the owner of the books and the room, he had done mischief in that house that would be discovered by and by. He also said his name was the Sage Muñaton."
"He must have said Friston," said Don Quixote.
"I don't know whether he called himself Friston or Friton," said the housekeeper, "only that his name ended in 'ton.'"

"So it does," said Don Quixote, "and he is a sage magician, a great enemy of mine, who has a grudge against me, because he knows by his arts and learning that in the course of time I am to engage in single combat with a knight he befriends, and that I am to defeat him, and he will be unable to prevent it; and for that reason he tries to do me every ill turn he can. But I promise him it will be hard for him to oppose or evade what is decreed by Heaven."

"Who doubts that?" said the niece; "but, uncle, who mixes you up in these quarrels? Wouldn't it be better to stay peacefully at home instead of roaming the world looking for better bread than ever came of wheat, never reflecting that many go for wool and come back shorn?"

"Oh, niece of mine," replied Don Quixote, "how wide of the mark you are in your reckoning: before they shear me I shall have plucked away and stripped off the beards of all who dare to touch so much as the tip of one of my hairs."
The two were unwilling to say anything more, as they could see his anger was kindling.

In short, he stayed quietly at home for fifteen days, showing no signs of wanting to take up his former delusions, and during that time he held lively discussions with his two friends, the curate and the barber, on his contention that what the world most needed was knights-errant, and that in him the revival of knight-errantry was to be accomplished. The curate sometimes contradicted him, sometimes went along with him, for if he had not taken that precaution he would have been unable to bring him to reason at all.

Meanwhile Don Quixote was working on a farm labourer, a neighbour of his, an honest man (if that title can be given to one who is poor), but with very little wit in his pate. In short, he so talked him over, with such persuasions and promises, that the poor clown made up his mind to ride out with him and serve as his squire. Don Quixote, among other things, told him he ought to be willing to go gladly, because any moment an adventure might occur that could win an island in the twinkling of an eye and leave him governor of it. On these and similar promises Sancho Panza (for that was the labourer's name) left wife and children and engaged himself as squire to his neighbour.

Don Quixote next set about raising some money; and by selling one thing, pawning another, and getting a bad bargain in every case, he scraped together a fair sum. He provided himself with a buckler, which he borrowed from a friend, and, patching up his battered helmet as best he could, he warned his squire Sancho of the day and hour he meant to set out, so Sancho could provide himself with what he thought most necessary. Above all, he ordered him to take saddlebags. Sancho said he would, and that he meant to take along a very good ass he had, since he was not much given to going on foot. About the ass, Don Quixote hesitated a little, trying to recall whether any knight-errant had ever taken with him a squire mounted on ass-back; but no example came to mind. Even so, he decided to take him, intending to provide him with a more honourable mount when the chance presented itself, by appropriating the horse of the first discourteous knight he came across. He provided himself with shirts and such other things as he could, following the host's advice; and all this being done, without taking leave — Sancho Panza of his wife and children, or Don Quixote of his housekeeper and niece — they rode out unseen by anyone from the village one night, and made such good progress over the course of it that by daylight they considered themselves safe from discovery even if a search were made.

Sancho rode on his ass like a patriarch, with his saddlebags and wine-flask, longing to see himself soon governor of the island his master had promised him. Don Quixote chose to take the same route and road he had taken on his first journey, that over the Campo de Montiel, which he travelled with less discomfort than the previous time; for, as it was early morning and the rays of the sun fell on them at an angle, the heat did not distress them.
And now Sancho Panza said to his master, "Your worship will be careful, Señor Knight-errant, not to forget about the island you've promised me, for be it ever so big I'll be equal to governing it."

To which Don Quixote replied, "You must know, friend Sancho Panza, that it was a very common practice among the knights-errant of old to make their squires governors of the islands or kingdoms they won, and I am determined that on my part there shall be no failure in so liberal a custom; on the contrary, I mean to improve upon it. They sometimes — and perhaps most often — waited until their squires were old, and then, when those squires had had enough of service and hard days and worse nights, they gave them some title or other, count or at most marquis, of some valley or province more or less. But if you live and I live, it may well be that before six days are out I shall have won some kingdom that has others depending on it, which will be just the thing to enable you to be crowned king of one of them. And don't think this remarkable, for things and chances fall to such knights in ways so unexampled and unforeseen that I might easily give you even more than I promise you."
"In that case," said Sancho Panza, "if I became a king by one of those miracles your worship speaks of, even Juana Gutierrez, my old woman, would come to be queen and my children infantes."
"Well, who doubts it?" said Don Quixote.

"I doubt it," replied Sancho Panza, "because for my part I'm convinced that even if God should shower down kingdoms on the earth, not one of them would fit the head of Mari Gutierrez. Let me tell you, señor, she isn't worth two maravedis for a queen; countess will fit her better, and that only with God's help."

"Leave it to God, Sancho," returned Don Quixote, "for he will give her what suits her best; but don't undervalue yourself so far as to be content with anything less than being governor of a province."
"I won't, señor," answered Sancho, "especially as I have a man of your quality for a master in your worship, who will know how to give me everything suitable for me and that I can carry."
